highlights:
The 2026 World Cup is finally here after what feels like an eternity of waiting, and next on the Group A fixture list following Thursday’s opener between Mexico and South Africa is a highly intriguing clash between South Korea and Czechia.

Czechia, meanwhile, finished second behind Croatia in their UEFA group and were forced into the playoffs, where they edged past both the Republic of Ireland and Denmark on penalties—results that highlight their resilience and capacity to grind out results under pressure.

On paper, South Korea should win. It not only has the stronger qualifying record, but also greater star power than Czechia—most notably LAFC forward Son Heung-min and Paris Saint-Germain’s Lee Kang-in. It also brings far more experience on the big stage, having qualified for every World Cup since 1986, while Czechia returns to the tournament for the first time since 2006.

South Korea ought to find that breakthrough, but it will not come easily—and Czechia will likely throw everything at it in the closing stages.

- Aerial threat: If Czechia is to trouble South Korea, it will likely come in the air. Its attacking options are all physically imposing, with several forwards standing well over six feet. Patrik Schick and Tomáš Chorý—at 6’3” and 6’6” respectively—pose a major aerial danger.

As mentioned, Czechia will likely look to play to its strengths, relying on attacking wingbacks who deliver crosses into the box for its physically dominant forwards.
[...]
That approach typically sees them line up in a 3-4-1-2 or 3-5-2 system, with David Jurásek on the left and Vladimír Coufal on the right, supporting a back three likely made up of Tomáš Holeš, Robin Hranáč and newly appointed captain Ladislav Krejčí.
[...]
In midfield, Tomáš Souček is expected to anchor the side alongside the experienced Vladimír Darida, with the pair providing both defensive protection and a significant aerial threat from deeper positions.
[...]
Up front, Patrik Schick is a guaranteed starter. If Czechia opts for 3-4-1-2, he will likely be partnered by Tomáš Chorý, with Pavel Šulc—the team’s creative maestro—operating as a No. 10. However, if it goes with an extra midfielder, Šulc will instead likely join the attack alongside Schick.

South Korea and Czech Republic begin their FIFA World Cup 2026 Group A campaigns at Guadalajara Stadium with both teams carrying useful unbeaten runs into the tournament. The matchup looks balanced, with South Korea offering stronger defensive trends and the Czech Republic bringing enough attacking quality to keep the contest close.
[...]
South Korea meet Czech Republic in Group A of the FIFA World Cup 2026 at Guadalajara Stadium, and the opening match should tell us plenty about how both sides intend to approach the section. South Korea arrive with a strong recent body of work under Myung-Bo Hong, while Czech Republic, coached by Miroslav Koubek, have also built a run of competitive resilience.
[...]
Czech Republic have plenty of reasons for confidence as well. They have been undefeated in 10 of their last 12 matches in all competitions and are unbeaten in their last 3. Their last 16 matches include 8 wins, with averages of 1.88 goals scored and 1.19 conceded, which points to a side capable of staying competitive even when matches become stretched.
[...]
The Czech Republic have also shown a tendency to produce close scorelines. They have drawn 50% of their last 6 matches, scoring 2 goals per game and conceding 0.83 during that period. That balance suggests they are not easy to pull apart, although South Korea’s pace in wide areas could test their defensive concentration.
[...]
The key question is whether South Korea’s sustained unbeaten trend can translate into a winning start against a Czech side that has become hard to defeat. South Korea have won by 2 or more goals in 50% of their last 12 matches, but Czech Republic have also won by 2 or more goals in 4 of their last 10, so both teams have shown they can take control when momentum shifts.
[...]
This looks more likely to be shaped by discipline and midfield control than by open attacking football. South Korea’s defensive numbers are slightly stronger, but Czech Republic’s recent draw rate and scoring consistency point toward a tight finish. The final outcome probability leans toward a draw at 35%, with fewer than 3 goals expected. Prediction: South Korea 1-1 Czech Republic in a careful start of the tournament for both teams, even though Forebet predicts South Korea to fall behind Mexico and the Czech Republic later on and be eliminated from the group.
